findings.statement: CXCR2 ranks first in convergence (meta-analysis upregulation [gene=CXCR2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.814]) but the corpus holds no extracted literature relation for it. Support is indirect: a network analysis named CXCL8 and its receptors CXCR1 and CXCR2 as primary therapeutic targets in UC, a herbal intervention lowered CXCL8, CXCR1 and CXCR2 in colonic tissue of UC mice, and CXCR2 was listed as a hub gene in active UC. Evidence is network or preclinical, not clinical in UC.

CXCL8 is strongly upregulated across cohorts (meta-analysis [gene=CXCL8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.864]). Literature states the axis of CXCL8 with its receptors CXCR1 and CXCR2 participates in UC pathogenesis through PI3K/Akt, MAPK and NF-kappaB signaling, and a blood RNA-seq validation ranked CXCL8 among the best diagnostic genes for IBD (not UC specific). CXCL8 is also a PPI hub gene in a UC bioinformatic study.

IDO1 is reported elevated in UC patients and correlated with M1 macrophage polarization in human data and colitis mice. IDO1 is said to induce M1 polarization via the ER stress GRP78-XBP1 pathway, and a methyl-tryptophan IDO inhibitor ameliorated DSS-induced weight loss, colonic shortening and disease severity. This is a single study in a mouse model; no clinical UC evidence in the corpus.

CHI3L1 is upregulated in UC patients and correlated with NLRP3 inflammasome expression; it is reported to promote macrophage pyroptosis via a BCAT1/NF-kappaB axis, and NF-kappaB activation reversed the protective effect of CHI3L1 inhibition. A drug-repurposing study confirmed velpatasvir binding to recombinant CHI3L1 by microscale thermophoresis (micromolar affinity). Evidence is preclinical and from few papers; CHI3L1 has no approved drug.

DUOX2 is among the most elevated proteins in inflamed UC biopsies versus healthy controls, and is listed with S100A8, IL-1B, CXCL1, MMP10 and others as a credible diagnostic and therapeutic biomarker. A herbal formula (TLXDS) is reported to alleviate UC by inhibiting DUOX2 overexpression, with the authors suggesting DUOX2 may be a key therapeutic target; this is a single preclinical study.

MMP10 is upregulated in active UC versus remission UC, Crohn disease and controls, and in preclinical UC compared with controls (prediagnostic samples). It is also in a candidate diagnostic biomarker panel. Consistent across several studies, but entirely expression/biomarker evidence with no therapeutic data.

AQP9 is predominantly expressed in neutrophils and upregulated in colon tissue of UC mice; it is reported to promote NET formation via JAK2-STAT3-mediated pyroptosis, aggravating epithelial injury, and was overexpressed in DSS and anti-CD40 colitis models. No drug exists for AQP9; evidence is one mechanistic mouse study plus a signature paper.

MMP1 is reported with strong diagnostic potential in a UC-associated CRC bioinformatic study, with ilomastat predicted in silico as an inhibitor. It is also among transcripts modified by mirikizumab that correlate with Mayo, Geboes and Robarts indices (with MMP3, S100A8, IL1B), linking it to treatment response. The diagnostic and drug claims are computational only.

SLC26A2 is down-regulated in the mucosa of active UC compared with healthy controls; decreased levels have diagnostic value and correlate with Mayo score and PUCAI. Single study, supporting that epithelial transporter loss is a replicated down-signal.

In tofacitinib non-responders, macrophages and fibroblasts increased in number and activation after treatment with upregulation of MMP9, IL1B, IL6, CXCL1, CXCL8 and S100A9 versus baseline, so these inflammatory myeloid/stromal genes flag non-response to JAK inhibition and their signal comes from infiltrating or activated immune cells rather than epithelium. IL-1B is also in a candidate diagnostic panel.

S100A9 expression showed excellent performance for diagnosing active UC in one study and is increased in UC by ONT-RNA-seq. It was downregulated in resident macrophages in tofacitinib response, and Atractylenolide-I is reported to target S100A9/AMPK/mTOR. The signal is largely myeloid.

LCN2 is increased in UC and IBD; its expression was higher in short-duration UC than long-duration UC and UC-associated cancer, but all were above normal, and it is proposed as a diagnostic biomarker for UC-associated carcinogenesis related to disease duration.

CD274 (PD-L1) has no extracted literature relation, despite a high Open Targets literature score. The corpus only shows it as a hub gene (with MMP1, NCF2, PLAU) positively associated with macrophage infiltration in UC, validated in GSE119600, and PD-L1 immunohistochemical validation in a Tokai University series. Checkpoint inhibitors in UC are not addressed.

caveats: Corpus is about 300 abstracts; many top-ranked genes (CXCR2, CXCR1, CD274, FCGR2A, JAK2, TREM1, INHBA, IL2RA) have zero extracted relations, so literature support there is only the Open Targets score.
Most gene-level literature evidence is bioinformatic hub-gene or signature work and single-lab mouse studies; no clinical trial in the corpus tests CXCR1/2, IDO1, CHI3L1, DUOX2 or AQP9 in UC.
The CXCL8 diagnostic performance comes from IBD blood data, not UC alone.
Several upregulated genes (S100A9, IL1B, CXCL8, MMP9) derive from infiltrating macrophages, neutrophils and fibroblasts, so expression is partly cell composition.
Tofacitinib is approved for UC, but the corpus shows its non-response is tied to macrophage activation (PMID 40320713).
PubMed connector requiring authorization was not used.
